What good is it to gain the whole world and lose your own life?
You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

e36.note: Philip the tetrarch named the city in honor of the emperor; today it is Banias. The cave and temple ruins once devoted to the god Pan still remain, and one of the main sources of the Jordan River springs up here.
e36.reflect: Jesus asked, “Who do you say I am?” Not repeating what others say, but with my own lips, who do I confess Jesus to be?

quiz.q: Which person was not among the answers the disciples reported when asked who people said Jesus was?
quiz.explain: The disciples reported that people called Jesus John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Mt 16:14). Moses is not mentioned.

e36.credit: James Tissot, Get Thee Behind Me Satan, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e37.title: Transfigured on the Mountain
e37.subtitle: Glory glimpsed for a moment on the mountain
story: Six days later, Jesus took only Peter, James, and John with him and climbed a high mountain. He had gone there to pray. As he prayed, his face shone like the sun, and his clothes flashed white as light. When the disciples, who had been struggling against sleep, opened their eyes, Moses and Elijah were talking with Jesus.

The two of them were speaking of his departure, which he was about to bring to fulfillment in Jerusalem. Not knowing what he was saying, Peter blurted out, Lord, it is good for us to be here. Let us build three shelters, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. Before he had even finished, a bright cloud covered them, and a voice spoke from the cloud. This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.

The disciples fell face down on the ground, trembling. Then Jesus came and touched them. Get up. Do not be afraid. When they looked up, there was no one there but Jesus alone. As they came down the mountain, Jesus told them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.

words.text: Get up. Do not be afraid.
Tell no one what you have seen until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.
Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but treated him however they pleased.
This is my Son, whom I love, my delight. Listen to him.

e37.note: The Gospels say only 'a high mountain.' Tradition has long identified it as Mount Tabor, but many scholars point to Mount Hermon, which is near Caesarea Philippi from the previous scene and much higher.
e37.reflect: On the shining mountain, the voice from heaven told the disciples, “Listen to him.” When the amazing moment has passed and I am back to ordinary days, how am I listening to his words?

quiz.q: Which two men appeared and talked with the transfigured Jesus?
quiz.explain: Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with Jesus (Mt 17:3; Mk 9:4; Lk 9:30).

e37.credit: James Tissot, The Transfiguration, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e38.title: Who Is the Greatest?
e38.subtitle: He sets a child in the middle of them
story: On the way back to Capernaum, the disciples were bickering in low voices behind him. When they came into the house, Jesus looked around at them and asked, what were you arguing about on the road? No one could say a word. They only hung their heads. Who was the greatest, that was what they had argued about.

Jesus sat down, called the twelve, and took a little child and stood the child in the middle of them. Then he took the child in his arms. Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all. Whoever welcomes one little child like this in my name welcomes me.

If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them wanders off, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go to look for the one that is lost? Then Peter came and asked, Lord, if my brother wrongs me, how many times must I forgive him? Seven times? Jesus answered. Not seven times, but seventy-seven times. And Jesus told them the story of a servant who was forgiven a huge debt, yet would not forgive a fellow servant a small one.

words.text: Whoever wants to be first must stand behind everyone else and become the servant of all.
Unless you turn around and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
Not just seven times. Forgive even seventy-seven times.

e38.note: In the parable, the servant was forgiven ten thousand talents, while his fellow servant owed him a hundred denarii. One talent was about six thousand days' wages for a laborer, an almost unimaginable contrast.
e38.reflect: To disciples arguing over who was the greatest, Jesus stood a little child among them and said the one who serves is great. Where do I long to be lifted up, and whom am I serving?

quiz.q: When Peter asked how many times he must forgive, what did Jesus answer?
quiz.explain: Jesus answered not seven times but seventy-seven times (Mt 18:22). The original can also be rendered 'seventy times seven,' and it means to forgive without end.

e38.credit: James Tissot, Jesus and the Little Child, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e39.title: Those Who Put Down Their Stones
e39.subtitle: The feast where he cried out for living water, and the words he wrote in the dust
story: As the Feast of Tabernacles drew near, Jerusalem filled with shelters woven from branches, and with pilgrims. It was a time when even his own brothers did not believe in him. Jesus went up quietly, without being seen, and when the feast was in full swing he appeared in the temple and began to teach. On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out in a loud voice. Anyone who is thirsty, come to me and drink.

The temple guards who had gone to arrest him came back empty handed. No one has ever spoken the way this man speaks. Early the next morning, as Jesus sat teaching in the temple courts, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees dragged before him a woman caught in adultery and stood her in the middle. Teacher, in the law Moses told us to stone such women. What do you say?

Jesus said nothing. He bent down and wrote something on the ground with his finger. When they kept pressing him, he straightened up. Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone. And again he bent down and wrote on the ground. One by one they went away, the oldest first, until only Jesus and the woman were left. Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you? No one, Lord. Neither do I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more.

words.text: If there is anyone among you who has no sin, let that person be the first to throw a stone at her.
Neither do I condemn you. Go, and from now on sin no more.
Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink. From the one who believes in me, living water will flow like a river.

e39.note: The story of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53 to 8:11, is missing from the earliest manuscripts. But it is regarded as an ancient tradition and appears in most Bibles, often set off with brackets or a note.
e39.reflect: When Jesus said, “Let the one without sin throw the first stone,” the people put down their stones one by one and left. Who am I condemning in my heart right now?

quiz.q: What did Jesus do when he bent down before the woman's accusers?
options: He looked up to heaven and prayed
He wrote on the ground with his finger
quiz.explain: Jesus bent down and wrote on the ground with his finger, and after he spoke, he bent down and wrote again (Jn 8:6, 8).

e39.credit: James Tissot, The Adulterous Woman--Christ Writing upon the Ground, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e40.title: Eyes Opened at Siloam
e40.subtitle: Eyes opened with mud and pool water
story: As Jesus walked along, his eyes fell on a man who had been blind from birth. His disciples asked, Teacher, why was this man born blind? Was it his own sin, or his parents'? Jesus answered. Neither this man sinned, nor his parents. This happened so that the works of God might be shown in him.

Jesus spat on the ground, worked the mud with his hands, and spread it on the man's eyes, and told him to go and wash in the pool of Siloam. Feeling his way, the man went down to the pool, scooped up water, and washed his face. When he lifted his wet eyelids, light poured in for the first time in his life. He came back seeing the road with his own eyes. That day was a Sabbath.

The Pharisees called him in and questioned him again and again. Even his parents, afraid of being thrown out of the synagogue, stepped back and told them to ask their grown son himself. But he would not back down. Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. There is one thing I do know. I was blind, and now I see. When he was finally thrown out, Jesus came looking for him and asked, do you believe in the Son of Man? Lord, I believe, he said, and he bowed down before him.

words.text: It was not his sin, nor his parents'. This happened so that the work of God might be shown through him.
While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.
Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam.
One thing I know for certain. I could not see, and now I can.

e40.note: In 2004, during sewer work in the south of Jerusalem, a stepped pool from the Second Temple period was discovered, and it is thought to be the Pool of Siloam in John's Gospel. Siloam means 'sent.'
e40.reflect: The man whose eyes were opened could not explain everything, but he testified, “I was blind, and now I see.” What is one grace of the Lord I can speak of with certainty?

quiz.q: According to John's Gospel, what does the name Siloam mean?
quiz.explain: John explains that Siloam means 'sent' (Jn 9:7).

e40.credit: James Tissot, The Blind Man Washes in the Pool of Siloam, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e41.title: The Good Samaritan and Two Sisters
e41.subtitle: One who becomes a neighbor, one who sits at his feet
story: A teacher of the law stood up to test Jesus. Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? Asked in return what was written in the law, he recited that one must love God with all one's heart and soul and strength and mind, and love one's neighbor as oneself. Your answer is right. Do this, and you will live. Wanting to justify himself, he asked again. And who is my neighbor?

Jesus told a story. A man going down from Jerusalem to Jericho fell among robbers, who stripped him, beat him, and left him half dead. A priest happened to be going down that road, and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. A Levite did the same. But a Samaritan traveling that way saw him and was moved with pity. He went to him, poured oil and wine on his wounds and bandaged them, then put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. Which one became a neighbor to that man? The one who showed him mercy, the teacher of the law answered. Go and do the same.

As they traveled on, Jesus came into a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home. Martha was rushing about with all the serving, while her sister Mary sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his words. At last Martha could bear it no longer and came to him. Lord, don't you care that my sister has left me to do the work alone? Martha, Martha. You are anxious and troubled about many things. But only one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, and it will not be taken from her.

words.text: Which of these three do you think became a neighbor to the man who fell among robbers?
Go and do the same.
Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about so many things. But only one thing is needed.
Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken from her.

e41.note: From Jerusalem to Jericho was about twenty-seven kilometers, a wilderness descent of more than a thousand meters. Luke says only 'a certain village,' but John's Gospel identifies the village of Martha and Mary as Bethany.
e41.reflect: The priest and the Levite passed by, but the Samaritan went to the wounded man and cared for him. Jesus said, “Go and do the same.” Who is the person I must not pass by today?

quiz.q: What money did the Samaritan give the innkeeper?
quiz.explain: The next day the Samaritan gave two denarii to the innkeeper and asked him to look after the man (Lk 10:35).

e41.credit: James Tissot, The Good Samaritan, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e42.title: I Am the Good Shepherd
e42.subtitle: The shepherd who calls his sheep by name
story: When the shepherd comes in through the gate and calls his own sheep by name, one by one, the sheep know his voice and follow him out. From a stranger's voice they only run away. With this familiar scene, Jesus spoke of himself. I am the gate for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

Before long it was winter, and Jerusalem was keeping the Feast of Dedication. As Jesus walked in Solomon's Colonnade in the temple, the Jewish leaders surrounded him. How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly. Jesus answered. I have told you already, and you do not believe. My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me. No one can snatch them out of my hand.

I and the Father are one. No sooner were the words spoken than people picked up stones again. When they tried to seize him, he slipped out of their grasp and withdrew across the Jordan to the place where John had first baptized, and he stayed there. Many people came to him. John never did a single sign, they said, but everything he said about this man was true. And there many believed in Jesus.

words.text: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.
I came so that the sheep may have life, and have it in overflowing abundance.
My sheep recognize my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
The Father and I are one.

e42.note: The Feast of Dedication is a winter festival commemorating how Judas Maccabeus, in 164 BC, recovered the Temple defiled by the foreign king Antiochus the Fourth and dedicated it again. Today it is Hanukkah.
e42.reflect: Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd; my sheep know my voice.” With so many voices around me these days, how am I recognizing his?

quiz.q: Where in the Temple was Jesus walking during the Feast of Dedication?
quiz.explain: It was winter, the Feast of Dedication, and Jesus was walking in Solomon's Porch in the Temple (Jn 10:22–23).

e42.credit: James Tissot, The Good Shepherd, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e43.title: The Joy of Finding the Lost
e43.subtitle: A sheep, a coin, and a son
story: Tax collectors and sinners were gathering around Jesus one by one to hear him. Watching this, the Pharisees and teachers of the law muttered. This man welcomes sinners, and even eats with them. Jesus told them parables, the stories of three people who would not stop until they had found what was lost.

A shepherd who lost one of his hundred sheep left the ninety-nine in the open country and searched until he found the lost one. When he found it, he joyfully carried it home on his shoulders and called his neighbors together. A woman who lost one of her ten silver coins lit a lamp, swept the whole house, and searched every corner. When at last she found it, she too called her friends and neighbors together. Rejoice with me. I have found the coin I lost.

A man's younger son took his share of the inheritance early, went off to a distant country, and squandered it all. On the day he would gladly have filled his stomach with the pods the pigs were eating, he came to his senses and turned back toward his father's house. While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, was filled with compassion, ran to him, and embraced him. The father threw a feast. This son of mine was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found. And to the older son, who came in from the field and in his anger refused to go inside, the father went out himself and pleaded with him.

words.text: There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who comes back than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.
This son of mine was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found. So let us celebrate together.
My child, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.

e43.note: Demanding an inheritance while one's father was still alive was considered a grave insult, and in a culture that prized dignity, an elderly head of the household running was a strange sight. Pigs were unclean animals to Jews.
e43.reflect: The father ran to embrace his returning son, but the older son was angry and would not go in to the feast. Where am I standing in this story?

quiz.q: How many silver coins did the woman in the parable have at first?
quiz.explain: The woman lost one of her ten drachmas, lit a lamp, and swept the house to find it (Lk 15:8).

e43.credit: James Tissot, The Return of the Prodigal Son, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e44.title: Lazarus, Come Out
e44.subtitle: The one who wept at the tomb and called death to give way
story: An urgent message came from Bethany. Lord, the one you love, Lazarus, is sick. Yet Jesus stayed where he was two more days. Only then did he say, let us go back to Judea. The disciples tried to stop him, reminding him that the people there had just tried to stone him. Then Thomas said to the other disciples, let us go too, so that we may die with him.

When he reached Bethany, Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days, and the house was full of people who had come to console the family. Hearing that Jesus was coming, Martha ran out to meet him. Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me will live, even though they die. Do you believe this? Yes, Lord, I believe. Then Mary came, fell at Jesus' feet, and wept. When he saw that even those who had come with her were weeping, Jesus wept too.

Jesus stood before the cave tomb sealed with a stone and told them to take the stone away. Martha said that after four days there would be a smell, but they rolled the stone away all the same. Jesus looked up to heaven and gave thanks to the Father. Then he cried out in a loud voice. Lazarus, come out. His hands and feet bound with linen strips and his face wrapped in a cloth, the man who had died walked out. After this, Caiaphas the high priest told the council that it was better for one man to die for the people. Those words became a prophecy that Jesus would die for the nation, to gather into one the scattered children of God.

words.text: I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me will live, though they die, and whoever lives believing in me will never die. Do you believe this?
Lazarus, come out!
Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?
Yes, Lord. I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, the one promised to come into the world.
Can’t you see it is to your advantage that one man should die in place of the people, so the whole nation is not destroyed?

e44.note: John writes that Bethany was fifteen stadia, about three kilometers, from Jerusalem. Later Jewish writings reflect the idea that the soul of the dead lingers near the body for three days, so four days was a time when hope had run out.
e44.reflect: At Lazarus's tomb, Jesus asked, “I am the resurrection and the life. Do you believe this?” Facing death and parting, how would I answer that question?

quiz.q: When Jesus arrived, how many days had Lazarus been in the tomb?
quiz.explain: When Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days (Jn 11:17, 39).

e44.credit: James Tissot, The Resurrection of Lazarus, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e45.title: The Children and the Rich Young Man
e45.subtitle: A kingdom received like a child, and hands that would not let go
story: In the land of Judea beyond the Jordan, crowds followed Jesus as well. When people brought little children for him to lay his hands on, the disciples blocked their way and scolded them. When Jesus saw this, he was displeased. Let the children come to me, and do not stop them. The kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Then he took the children in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them.

As Jesus was setting out again, a man came running up. Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? When Jesus told him the commandments, the man, still on his knees, said he had kept them all since he was a boy. Jesus looked at him closely and loved him. You still lack one thing. Go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.

At these words his face fell, and he went away grieving, for he had great wealth. Jesus looked around at his disciples and said, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. The disciples were astonished and said to one another, then who can be saved? Jesus looked at them and said, for people it is impossible, but for God all things are possible.

words.text: Let the little children come to me. Do not stop them. The kingdom of God belongs to such as these.
You lack one thing. Sell what you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.
By human strength it cannot be done. But not so with God. Nothing is impossible for God.

e45.note: After raising Lazarus, Jesus stayed for a while in Ephraim near the wilderness, then went to the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Matthew calls the man young, Luke a ruler, Mark a man of great wealth, so he is often called the rich young ruler.
e45.reflect: When the rich young man was told to leave what he had and follow, he went away sad. On the road of following Jesus, what am I still clutching and unable to let go?

quiz.q: Which animal did Jesus say could pass through the eye of a needle more easily than a rich person could enter the kingdom of God?
quiz.explain: It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (Mt 19:24; Mk 10:25; Lk 18:25).

e45.credit: James Tissot, The Rich Young Man Went Away Sorrowful, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e46.title: Two Encounters in Jericho
e46.subtitle: A cry from the roadside and a gaze up into a tree
story: By the dusty roadside of Jericho, blind Bartimaeus sat begging. As the crowd going up to Jerusalem passed by in a buzz of voices, he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing, and he cried out. Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me. People scolded him and told him to be quiet, but he shouted all the louder.

Jesus stopped and told them to call him. Take heart. Get up. He is calling you. Throwing off his cloak, he sprang to his feet and came to Jesus. What do you want me to do for you? Teacher, I want to see again. Go. Your faith has made you well. At that moment his eyes were opened, and he followed Jesus along the road.

In that city lived a chief tax collector named Zacchaeus, and he was rich. He wanted to see Jesus, but he was short and the crowd hid him from view, so he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore fig tree. When Jesus reached the spot, he stopped, looked up, and called to him. Zacchaeus, hurry and come down. Today I must stay at your house. He came down quickly and welcomed Jesus with joy, and said he would give half of his possessions to the poor. On this road Jesus had already told them, the Son of Man came to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

words.text: Zacchaeus, hurry and come down. Today I must stay at your house.
The Son of Man came to seek out and save those who are lost.
What would you like me to do for you?
Go. Your faith has made you well.
The Son of Man came not to be waited on but to serve others, and to give up his life as a ransom for many.

e46.note: Jericho is an oasis city about 250 meters below sea level. Herod had a winter palace there, and because it stood on the route of the date palm and balsam trade, its customs office was important. The Gospels differ slightly in the number of blind men and the timing.
e46.reflect: Bartimaeus shouted all the louder when people scolded him, and Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Jesus. What is keeping me from coming to Jesus?

quiz.q: What kind of tree did Zacchaeus climb to see Jesus?
quiz.explain: Zacchaeus was short, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore fig tree (Lk 19:4).

e46.credit: James Tissot, Zacchaeus in the Sycamore Awaiting the Passage of Jesus, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e47.title: The Perfume at Bethany
e47.subtitle: A broken jar, and the fragrance of love filling the house
story: On the evening six days before Passover, a dinner was held in Bethany, the hillside village east of Jerusalem. Lazarus, who had died and come back to life, sat at the table with the guests, and Martha bustled about serving the food. Mark tells us this dinner took place in the house of Simon, who had once had leprosy. Beneath the lamplight, the talk went back and forth in low voices.

Then Mary came in quietly, holding close an alabaster jar with a pound of costly pure nard. She broke the jar and poured the perfume over Jesus' head, then poured it on his feet too and wiped them with her loosened hair. The heavy fragrance filled the whole house. People held their breath, and no one dared to speak first.

This perfume could have been sold for three hundred denarii. Why wasn't it given to the poor? The sharp voice of Judas Iscariot broke the silence. He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he kept the money bag and used to help himself to what was put in it. Jesus came to the woman's defense. Leave her alone. She has kept this for the day of my burial. The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have me.

words.text: Leave her alone. Why are you troubling her? She has done a beautiful thing for me.
She did all she could. She has anointed my body ahead of time for its burial.
The poor will always be with you, but you will not always have me.
Listen closely. Wherever the good news is told in all the world, what she has done will be told too, and she will be remembered.

e47.note: Nard was a precious perfume drawn from the root of a plant that grows in the Himalayas. A day's wage was one denarius, so three hundred denarii was a fortune, nearly a full year of a laborer's work.
e47.reflect: Mary poured out costly perfume without holding back, and Jesus said, “She has done what she could.” What can I give the Lord without counting the cost?

quiz.q: How much did Judas say the perfume could have been sold for?
quiz.explain: In Jn 12:5 Judas names three hundred denarii. Thirty pieces of silver was the price Judas was paid for handing Jesus over (Mt 26:15).

e47.credit: James Tissot, The Ointment of the Magdalene, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e48.title: The Procession of Palms
e48.subtitle: A king on a young donkey, weeping over the city
story: They had come to the foot of the Mount of Olives, near Bethphage and Bethany. Jesus sent two disciples into the village ahead and told them, you will find a colt tied there that no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you why, say, the Lord needs it. When the disciples brought the colt and threw their cloaks on its back, Jesus quietly sat on it.

Pilgrims who had come for Passover spread their cloaks on the road and came out carrying palm branches. Hosanna. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. The shouts rolled down the slope of the Mount of Olives and echoed up to the city walls. Some Pharisees in the crowd pressed him. Teacher, rebuke your disciples. Jesus answered. If they keep quiet, the stones will cry out.

As the road turned downhill and the city spread out before him, Jesus looked at it and wept. If only you had known on this day the way to peace. But now it is hidden from your eyes. This cheering city, not recognizing the time when God had come to it, was walking toward the ruin that was coming.

words.text: If only you had known, even today, the way that leads to peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes.
I tell you, if these fall silent, the very stones by the road will cry out instead.
For you did not recognize the time when God came to visit you.
If anyone asks why you are doing this, say, The Lord has need of it.

e48.note: Zechariah 9:9 foretold that the king of Zion would come humbly, riding on a donkey. Matthew and John read this entry as the fulfillment of that prophecy. Palm branches stood for national victory and liberation.
e48.reflect: The crowd shouted “Hosanna,” expecting a king, but Jesus came riding on a donkey. Am I following the Jesus I want him to be, or Jesus as he came?

quiz.q: What did Jesus ride as he entered Jerusalem?
quiz.explain: He rode the young donkey the disciples brought, with their cloaks laid on it (Mk 11:7; Jn 12:14). It recalls the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9.

e48.credit: James Tissot, The Procession on the Mount of Olives, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e49.title: A House of Prayer
e49.subtitle: Overturned tables, a courtyard opened again for prayer
story: Early the next morning, on the way up from Bethany to Jerusalem, Jesus was hungry. Seeing a fig tree in full leaf in the distance, he went up to it. He looked up into its branches, but there was nothing but leaves, not a single fig. It was not the season for figs. Jesus said to the tree, from now on, may no one ever eat fruit from you again. The disciples took note of what he said.

As he entered the outer court of the temple, a din like a marketplace met him. Coins jingled, doves fluttered, haggling shouts flew back and forth. Jesus drove out those who were buying and selling, and overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. He would not let anyone carry goods across the temple courts. My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations. But you have made it a den of robbers.

Into the courtyard, now quiet again, came the blind and the lame, and Jesus healed them. Children in the temple courts shouted at the top of their voices. Hosanna to the Son of David. The chief priests and the teachers of the law looked for a way to get rid of him. But they could do nothing, because all the people hung on his words.

words.text: Is it not written, My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations? But you have turned it into a den of robbers.
Yes, I hear them. Have you never read, From the lips of children and infants you have brought praise to perfection?
From now on and forever, may no one ever eat fruit from you again.

e49.note: The outer court of the Temple was the Court of the Gentiles, open even to non-Jews. Pilgrims bought their sacrifices here, and are known to have exchanged money for Tyrian shekels to pay the Temple tax.
e49.reflect: Jesus drove out the traders, saying, “My house will be a house of prayer.” Is my worldly busyness crowding out deep fellowship with God?

quiz.q: What did Jesus say the people had made of the Temple?
quiz.explain: Quoting Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, Jesus rebuked them for turning the house of prayer into a den of robbers (Mk 11:17).

e49.credit: James Tissot, The Accursed Fig Tree, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e50.title: Questions in the Temple Courts
e50.subtitle: Questions set as traps, answers that came back as love
story: The temple courts were taut with sharp questions. Pharisees and Herodians came up to Jesus. Teacher, is it right to pay taxes to the emperor, or not? It was a trap set to catch him whichever way he answered. Jesus had them bring him a denarius. Whose face is this, and whose inscription? The emperor's, they answered, and Jesus said, give to the emperor what belongs to the emperor, and to God what belongs to God.

Next came the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, with a story about a woman who married seven brothers one after another. A teacher of the law who had been listening to the exchange stepped forward and asked, which commandment is the first of all? Jesus' answer was astonishingly simple. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and soul and mind and strength. And love your neighbor as yourself.

When the arguments had died down, Jesus sat down opposite the offering box and watched people putting in their money. The rich passed by, dropping in heavy sums. Then a poor widow came up and quietly let fall two small coins. Jesus called his disciples and said, this widow has put in more than anyone. They all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had to live on.

words.text: Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and give to God what belongs to God.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, all your mind and all your strength. The second is this: love your neighbor as yourself.
This poor widow has given more than anyone. The others gave a little from their plenty, but she gave everything she had to live on.
God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

e50.note: The denarius of the time is thought to have carried the face of Emperor Tiberius and words honoring him as son of a god. The lepton the widow gave was the smallest coin in circulation.
e50.reflect: Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus said to love God with all your heart and to love your neighbor as yourself. What place do these two loves hold in my day today?

quiz.q: What did the poor widow put into the offering box?
quiz.explain: The widow put in two lepta, worth a single quadrans (Mk 12:42; Lk 21:2). Jesus said she had given more than anyone.

e50.credit: James Tissot, The Tribute Money, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e51.title: The Last Days, Seen from the Mount of Olives
e51.subtitle: Stones that will fall, and words that will never pass away
story: As they were leaving the temple, one of the disciples stopped and marveled. Teacher, look. What enormous stones, and what magnificent buildings. The great stone walls blazed in the sunlight. But Jesus looked at those walls and spoke calmly. Not one stone here will be left on another. Every one will be thrown down.

Toward evening, Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives, facing the temple. Peter, James, John, and Andrew came to him quietly. When will these things happen? Jesus spoke of wars and earthquakes and famines. He told them of those who would lead people astray, and of the persecution to come. But whoever endures to the end will be saved.

About that day or hour no one knows, not the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. So stay awake. The stories of the wise bridesmaids who took oil along with their lamps, of the servant who made more from the talents entrusted to him, of those who gave food and drink to the least of these, drifted low over the darkening city.

words.text: Heaven and earth will one day pass away. But my words will remain to the end.
Keep alert and stay awake. You do not know when the time will come.
I tell you the truth: whatever you did for the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.
Do you see these great buildings? Not one stone here will be left on another. Every one will be thrown down.

e51.note: The Temple, greatly expanded by Herod, was burned and destroyed in AD 70 by the Roman army under Titus. The Western Wall in Jerusalem today is part of the retaining wall that held up the Temple Mount.
e51.reflect: Jesus said no one knows the day or the hour, so stay awake. If the Lord came today, what would he find me doing?

quiz.q: Which story does not appear in Matthew 25?
quiz.explain: Matthew 25 tells, one after another, of the ten bridesmaids, the talents, and the sheep and the goats (Mt 25:1–46). The prodigal son is a parable in Luke 15.

e51.credit: James Tissot, The Prophecy of the Destruction of the Temple, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e52.title: The Last Supper in the Upper Room
e52.subtitle: The last night, when he washed their feet and broke the bread
story: On the first day of Unleavened Bread, Peter and John met a man in the city carrying a jar of water and followed him. In the house he entered was a large upper room, furnished and ready, and there they prepared the Passover table. When evening came and the disciples had gathered around, Jesus got up, took off his outer robe, and tied a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into a basin and washed their feet one by one, drying them with the towel.

In the middle of the meal, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them. This is my body, given for you. Then he took the cup and handed it to them. This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. Then he said in a low voice, one of you will betray me. As the room froze, Judas took the piece of bread, got up, and went out. It was night.

To the disciples who remained, Jesus spoke for a long time. Love one another, just as I have loved you. Do not let your hearts be troubled. I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Then he lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed to the Father for them. After singing a hymn, they went out into the dark toward the Mount of Olives.

words.text: This is my body, given for you. Do this to remember me. This cup is my blood, the blood of God’s covenant, poured out so that the sins of many may be forgiven.
I give you a new command: love one another. As I have loved you, so love one another. By this everyone will know you are my disciples.
I am the way, the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
Peace I leave with you. My own peace I give you, not as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not be afraid.

e52.note: Matthew, Mark and Luke present this supper as a Passover meal, while John says Jesus was crucified on the day of preparation for Passover. Scholars still discuss how the two accounts fit together.
e52.reflect: Jesus washed his disciples' feet and said, “Love one another as I have loved you.” Who is the person I should humble myself to serve today?

quiz.q: Which two disciples were sent to prepare the Passover meal?
quiz.explain: Lk 22:8 says Jesus sent Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal.

e52.credit: James Tissot, The Last Supper, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e53.title: The Night in Gethsemane
e53.subtitle: Not my will, but yours
story: That night, after the supper, they crossed the Kidron Valley and entered the garden of Gethsemane at the foot of the Mount of Olives. Moonlight seeped faintly through the olive trees. Jesus took only Peter, James, and John and went in deeper. Then he began to be deeply distressed and troubled. My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow, to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch with me.

About a stone's throw away, he fell to the ground. Father, if it is possible, take this cup away from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will. His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. When he came back, he found the disciples asleep, exhausted from sorrow. Could you not keep watch with me for one hour? Three times he went off alone to pray, and came back.

Then torches flickered out of the darkness beyond, and a crowd came pressing in with swords and clubs. At its head was Judas. He called out, Rabbi, and kissed Jesus. Peter drew his sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant, Malchus. Jesus said, no more of this, and touched the ear and healed it. When the crowd seized Jesus, all the disciples deserted him and ran away.

words.text: Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Take this cup from me. Yet let it be not what I want, but what you want.
My soul is crushed with grief, to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.
Stay awake and pray, so you do not give in to temptation. The spirit is willing, but the body is weak.
Put your sword back in its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup the Father has handed me?

e53.note: Gethsemane is usually explained as meaning olive press. It was an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives, and Luke and John say Jesus often went there with his disciples.
e53.reflect: In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed for this cup to be taken away, then said, “Father, let your will be done.” What prayer do I need to pour out honestly to God right now and leave in his hands?

quiz.q: What was the name of the high priest's servant whose ear Peter cut off?
quiz.explain: Jn 18:10 gives the servant's name as Malchus and says he lost his right ear. Luke records that Jesus healed the ear (Lk 22:51).

e53.credit: James Tissot, My Soul is Sorrowful unto Death, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e54.title: Silence at the Trial
e54.subtitle: A silent king, and a denial spoken three times
story: With his hands bound, Jesus was taken first to Annas, and then to the house of Caiaphas the high priest. Late into the night witnesses stood up, but their stories did not agree. The high priest pressed him, but he stayed silent. The high priest asked again. Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One? Jesus answered. I am. The high priest tore his clothes, and the council cried out that he deserved to die.

At that same hour, down in the courtyard, Peter sat warming himself by a charcoal fire. A servant girl stared at him and said, this man was with him too. Peter denied it. I do not know the man. At the very moment he denied it for the third time, the rooster crowed. The Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter went outside and wept bitterly.

At daybreak the council bound Jesus and handed him over to Pilate the governor. Pilate said, I find no guilt in this man. Sending him to Herod changed nothing. The crowd shouted all the louder. Crucify him! In the end Pilate took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd. He released Barabbas, and after having Jesus flogged, handed him over to be crucified.

words.text: Yes, I am he. And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Mighty One, coming with the clouds of heaven.
My kingdom does not belong to this world. If it did, my people would fight to keep me from being handed over.
I was born and came into the world for this: to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.

e54.note: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36. In 1961 a stone inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea on the Mediterranean coast.
e54.reflect: Peter, who had promised to follow to the end, was so afraid that he denied knowing Jesus three times. When do I find myself pretending not to know Jesus because I fear how others will see me?

quiz.q: Which prisoner did Pilate release at the crowd's demand?
quiz.explain: Following the custom of releasing one prisoner at the feast, Pilate freed Barabbas, who had been jailed for rebellion and murder (Mk 15:6–15; Lk 23:19, 25).

e54.credit: James Tissot, Behold the Man, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e55.title: Golgotha
e55.subtitle: The day it was finished, and the stillness of the tomb
story: The soldiers dressed Jesus in a purple robe and pressed a crown woven of thorns onto his head. Hail, king of the Jews! On the road out of the city, Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, was seized and made to carry the cross in his place. At Golgotha, which means the place of the skull, they nailed Jesus to the cross. It was nine in the morning. The notice above his head read, the King of the Jews.

At noon darkness came over the whole land and lasted until three in the afternoon. On either side of him two criminals hung with him. Jesus prayed. Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing. To the criminal who repented he said, today you will be with me in paradise, and his mother, standing nearby, he entrusted to the disciple he loved. At last Jesus cried out with a loud voice and breathed his last. At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.

At dusk, as the Sabbath drew near, Joseph of Arimathea went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. He was a member of the council, but a disciple who had followed Jesus in secret. Nicodemus came too, bringing about a hundred pounds of myrrh mixed with aloes. The two men took down the body, wrapped it in fine linen with the spices, and laid it in a new tomb cut in the rock, in a garden. A great stone was rolled across the entrance of the tomb.

words.text: Father, forgive them. They do not know what they are doing.
I promise you, this very day you will be with me in paradise.
Woman, here is your son. And you, take her now as your mother.
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I am thirsty.
It is finished.
Father, into your hands I entrust my spirit.

e55.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful death Rome dealt out, reserved for rebels and slaves. Tradition most strongly places Golgotha at the site of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Garden Tomb, proposed in the nineteenth century, is also known as a place of pilgrimage.
e55.reflect: On the cross, Jesus prayed for those nailing him there: “Father, forgive them.” Thinking of someone I have not yet forgiven, what can I pray?

quiz.q: Whom did the soldiers force to carry the cross of Jesus?
quiz.explain: The soldiers forced Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, to carry the cross (Mk 15:21; Lk 23:26). Mark names him as the father of Alexander and Rufus.

e55.credit: James Tissot, What Our Lord Saw from the Cross, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e56.title: Mary
e56.when: First day of the week · Dawn
e56.subtitle: The voice that calls her by name
story: On the first day of the week, at dawn, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb and saw that the stone had been moved from the entrance. She ran to tell them, and Peter and the beloved disciple came racing to the tomb, out of breath. Inside lay only the linen cloths, and the cloth that had been around his head was folded up in a place by itself.

Even after the disciples had gone home, Mary stood outside the tomb weeping. As she wept, she bent down to look inside, and there sat two angels in white, one at the head and one at the feet of where the body had lain. Woman, why are you weeping? Mary answered. They have taken my Lord away, and I do not know where they have put him. As she said this, she turned around and saw someone standing there. Blinded by her tears, she took him for the gardener.

Mary. A familiar voice called her name. Mary turned and cried out in Hebrew, Rabboni! which means Teacher. She ran to the disciples with the news. I have seen the Lord! On the morning of the resurrection, that joy began to spread from the lips of one woman.

words.text: Mary.
Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?
Do not hold on to me; I have not yet gone up to the Father. Go and tell my brothers: I am going up to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.
I have seen the Lord!

e56.note: Magdala was a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Luke says Jesus drove seven demons out of Mary Magdalene, and that she supported Jesus and his companions out of her own means.
e56.reflect: Weeping Mary recognized Jesus when he called her by name. In my sorrow, where am I hearing the Lord's voice calling me?

quiz.q: Who did Mary at first think the risen Jesus was?
quiz.explain: Mary took Jesus for the gardener and asked where he had put the body (Jn 20:15). Only when he called her name did she recognize him (Jn 20:16).

e56.credit: James Tissot, Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e57.title: The Road to Emmaus
e57.when: First day of the week · Afternoon
e57.subtitle: Hearts on fire, and bread broken
story: That afternoon, two disciples were walking to Emmaus, a village about sixty stadia from Jerusalem. As they talked over everything that had happened in the past few days, their voices were heavy. Then a traveler came up and walked along beside them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. The traveler asked, what is this you are discussing with each other as you walk along?

The two stopped, their faces downcast. Cleopas said, we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel. Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, the traveler explained to them, one by one, what was said about himself in all the scriptures. When they reached the village, the sun was going down, and the traveler acted as if he were going on. The two held him back. It is nearly evening. Stay with us.

When they sat down at the table, he took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and handed it to them. At that moment their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. But at once Jesus vanished from their sight. Were not our hearts burning within us while he talked with us on the road and opened the scriptures to us? They got up that very hour and retraced the dark road by night, back to Jerusalem.

words.text: How foolish you are, and how slow of heart to believe all the prophets said! Did not the Christ have to suffer these things and then enter his glory?
What are you talking about with each other as you walk along?
Weren't our hearts burning like fire within us while he talked with us on the road and opened the scriptures to us?

e57.note: The exact location of Emmaus is unknown. To fit the record of about eleven kilometers from Jerusalem, Motza and Qubeibeh have been proposed, and one tradition points to the more distant Emmaus Nicopolis.
e57.reflect: As the two discouraged disciples walked, their hearts burned while Jesus opened the Scriptures to them. What word has set my heart on fire again?

quiz.q: Which of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus is named?
quiz.explain: Lk 24:18 gives the name of one of them as Cleopas. The other is not named.

e57.credit: James Tissot, The Pilgrims of Emmaus on the Road, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e58.title: Through the Locked Door
e58.when: That night, and eight days later
e58.subtitle: Peace that came through a locked door
story: On the evening of the day of resurrection, the disciples were gathered in one room with the doors locked tight, for fear of the Jewish leaders. Just as the two back from Emmaus were telling their story, Jesus stood among them. Peace be with you. Startled and frightened, the disciples were sure they were seeing a ghost.

He showed them his hands and feet, marked by the nails, and his side. While they still could not believe it for joy and amazement, he took a piece of broiled fish and ate it in front of them. Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures and said, the Christ will suffer and rise again, and the message of forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations. Then he breathed on them and said, receive the Holy Spirit.

The disciples told Thomas, who had not been there, we have seen the Lord. Thomas shook his head. Unless I see the nail marks in his hands and touch them, I will not believe. Eight days later, in the room with the doors locked again, Jesus stood and held out his hands and his side to Thomas. A confession burst from Thomas's lips. My Lord and my God!

words.text: Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so now I am sending you.
Look at my hands and my feet. It is really me. Touch me and see. A ghost does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.
You believe because you have seen me. Truly blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe.
My Lord and my God!
The Christ had to suffer and rise from death on the third day. Now, in his name, the call to turn back and be forgiven will spread from Jerusalem to every nation.

e58.note: Thomas was called Didymus, meaning the Twin. In Jewish reckoning, eight days later counts the first day too, so it points to the same day of the following week, the first day of the week come round again.
e58.reflect: Thomas, who had doubted, stood before the risen Jesus and confessed, “My Lord and my God!” With doubts still lingering, what do I want to confess to Jesus now?

quiz.q: When did Jesus appear again, this time with Thomas present?
quiz.explain: Jn 20:26 says that eight days later, when the disciples were gathered again with Thomas among them, Jesus stood inside the locked doors.

e58.credit: James Tissot, The Disbelief of Saint Thomas, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e59.title: Morning on the Shore of Tiberias
e59.subtitle: Love, asked three times beside a charcoal fire
story: One day, back by the Sea of Galilee, Simon Peter said, I am going fishing. Thomas and Nathanael, the sons of Zebedee, and two other disciples said they would go with him, and they got into the boat. All night they cast their nets, but caught nothing. Just as day was breaking, someone was standing on the shore.

When they did as he said and cast the net on the right side of the boat, so many fish were caught that they could not haul it in. The beloved disciple cried out to Peter, it is the Lord! Peter threw on his outer garment and jumped straight into the water. When they came ashore, there was fish on a charcoal fire, and bread as well. There were one hundred fifty-three large fish in the net they hauled up, and yet the net was not torn.

After breakfast, beside the charcoal fire, Jesus asked Peter, Simon son of John, do you love me? When the same question came a third time, Peter was hurt. Lord, you know everything. You know that I love you. Jesus said, feed my sheep. And follow me.

words.text: Simon son of John, do you love me? Then feed my flock.
Follow me.
Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find fish.
Come and have breakfast.

e59.note: In John's Gospel the word for a charcoal fire appears only twice: in the courtyard of the high priest's house where Peter denied Jesus, and on this morning. Three denials are followed by three confessions of love.
e59.reflect: Jesus asked Peter, who had denied him three times, “Do you love me?” three times, and entrusted him with his work again. If the Lord asked me the same where I have fallen, what would I want to answer?

quiz.q: How many large fish were in the net the disciples hauled in?
quiz.explain: Jn 21:11 says there were a hundred and fifty-three large fish, and even with so many the net was not torn.

e59.credit: James Tissot, Christ Appears on the Shore of Lake Tiberias, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e60.title: The Last Charge on the Mountain
e60.subtitle: The promise to be with them to the end of the age
story: The eleven disciples went to Galilee and climbed the mountain Jesus had told them about. In the wind that swept the ridge, each carrying his own failure and fear, they waited for him in silence. It was just as the women had been told on their way back from the tomb. Go to Galilee. There you will see me.

When at last Jesus appeared, the disciples bowed down and worshiped him. Yet even then some among them doubted. Even on the same mountain, each heart was different. A moment of silence passed among those bowed on the ground. Jesus came near to them, just as they were, and spoke.

All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations. Baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teach them to keep everything I have commanded you. Before a small company in which doubt and faith were mixed, the whole world lay open. And one last promise remained. Look, I am with you always, to the very end of the age.

words.text: So go and make disciples of all nations. Baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and teach them to keep all I commanded.
Remember this: I am with you always, to the very end of the age.
All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

e60.note: Matthew's Gospel opens with the Immanuel prophecy, God is with us, and closes with the promise, I am with you always. Which mountain this was is not recorded.
e60.reflect: Though some still doubted, Jesus told them, “Go and make disciples of all nations,” and promised to be with them. What has he entrusted to me, as lacking as I am?

quiz.q: In Matthew 28, how many disciples went to the mountain in Galilee and met Jesus?
quiz.explain: The eleven disciples, without Judas Iscariot, went to the mountain in Galilee where Jesus had told them to go (Mt 28:16).

e60.credit: James Tissot, The Exhortation to the Apostles, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain

e61.title: Into the Cloud
e61.subtitle: A blessing and a promise left at his parting
story: For forty days after he rose, Jesus appeared to the disciples many times and spoke to them about the kingdom of God. That day he led them out of the city and walked with them as far as the outskirts of Bethany. The disciples asked one last question. Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?

It is not for you to know the times or seasons the Father has set. But when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, you will receive power, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. When he had finished speaking, he lifted up his hands and blessed them, and while he was blessing them, he was taken up into heaven. A cloud hid him, and they saw him no more.

As the disciples stood gazing up at the sky, two men dressed in white stood beside them. Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up into the sky? This Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you saw him go. The disciples returned to Jerusalem filled with great joy. And every day they were in the temple, praising God.

words.text: When the Holy Spirit comes on you, you will receive power. You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
It is not for you to know the times or seasons the Father has set by his own authority.
Men of Galilee, why do you stand staring at the sky? This Jesus, taken from you into heaven, will come back just as you saw him go.

e61.note: Acts says that after the Ascension the disciples returned from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's walk away. Bethany is a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives.
e61.reflect: Before he ascended to heaven, Jesus said, “You will be my witnesses to the ends of the earth.” Right where I stand today, to whom am I showing him?

quiz.q: What hid Jesus from sight as he was taken up into heaven?
quiz.explain: Acts 1:9 says that as Jesus was taken up, a cloud hid him from the disciples' sight.

e61.credit: James Tissot, The Ascension, c. 1886–1894 · Brooklyn Museum · Public domain
